question.text: An oscillator of mass <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>M</mi></math> is at rest in its equilibrium position in a potential, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>k</mi><msup><mfenced separators="|"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi> </mi><mo>–</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></math> . A particle of mass <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>m</mi></math> comes from the right with speed <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>u</mi></math> and collides completely inelastic with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>M</mi></math> and sticks to it. This process repeats every time the oscillator crosses its equilibrium position. The amplitude of oscillations after <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>13</mn></math> collisions is: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfenced><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced></math>
